column4: The verse describes a slain man whose killing is disputed and concealed, then says God will bring what they conceal to light. This is a direct murder-investigation parallel to the section’s divided oath among a victim’s kin.

The next ayah commands an act involving the slain person and states that God gives life to the dead and shows signs; its own stated contribution is the sign of resurrection, completing the preceding murder-dispute scene without itself describing the kin’s oath.

In a different family-law case, a husband answers an accusation with four sworn testimonies and a fifth invoking God’s curse if he lies. This is a specific parallel to the section’s oath procedure among a murdered person’s guardians, though it concerns an accusation between spouses.
This ayah supplies the husband’s fifth oath and its consequence, continuing the fixed family testimony procedure begun in 24:6.
The wife may avert the prescribed penalty by giving four sworn testimonies against her husband’s charge; the oath procedure turns to the accused family member’s answer.
The fifth testimony invokes God’s wrath if the husband is truthful, closing the reciprocal oath procedure in this distinct family-law setting.
The command to testify justly even against oneself, parents, or close relatives is a direct boundary on a kin-based claim: the duty is truthful justice even when the testimony harms one’s own family.
The verse forbids allowing hatred of a people to make one unjust; this is a specific restraint on the vengeance and excess that can attach to a blood claim.
The verse uses the section’s م ث ل root for evil repaid with its like, giving a direct Qur’anic wording for measured recompense.

The verse says corruption appeared on land and sea because of what people’s hands earned, so they taste some of their deeds. This directly joins the section’s corrupting peoples to the punishment poured upon them.

The delayed punishment is questioned as though something were holding it back, but when it comes nothing turns it aside; this closely develops the section’s image of a return held ready at the mirsad.
God is not unaware of wrongdoers; He only postpones them to a day when eyes stare. This directly explains the section’s waiting image as deferred, not forgotten, recompense.
The verse warns disbelievers not to mistake their respite for good, since the delay lets them increase in sin before humiliating punishment; it gives a moral reason for the section’s kept account.

God does not immediately seize people for their wrongdoing, but postpones them to a stated term; when it arrives, it cannot be delayed. This is a specific parallel to recompense held until its appointed time.
If God took people at once for what they earned, no creature would remain, but He postpones them to a term; the verse makes the section’s watchful delay explicit.
When punishment reaches Pharaoh’s people, they ask Moses to invoke God and promise to believe if it is removed; this begins a concrete account of punishment held pending their response.
After the affliction is removed until an appointed term, Pharaoh’s people break their promise; this ayah shows wrongdoing continuing during reprieve.
The next ayah says God took retribution from them and drowned them, completing the delayed return in Pharaoh’s example.
God seizes Pharaoh as نَكَال, a punishment made an example, directly joining the section’s Pharaoh exemplar to the dictionary sense of exemplary penalty.
The following ayah calls that event a lesson for those who fear, stating explicitly what the section’s exemplary punishments are for.
This ayah names Ad and Thamud and points to their dwellings, recalling the same earlier peoples whose transgression and punishment the section treats as precedents.
The next ayah brings in Pharaoh among arrogant people who rejected clear proofs; the following 29:40 completes their seizure, so this is the named Pharaoh contribution to that punishment sequence.
The verse says each group was seized for its sin by a fitting mode and that God did not wrong them; this is a concise account of the section’s precedent punishments and just return.
This ayah names Thamud and Ad as deniers of the striking calamity, setting up the distinct punishments narrated for them in 69:5–8.
The next account specifies that Ad’s wind lasted seven nights and eight days, giving duration and physical force to the punishment of a people named in the section.
The account asks whether any remnant of Ad can be seen after the wind, completing the example as a destruction that leaves no people behind.
After Thamud hamstring the she-camel, they are given only three days’ respite before the promised punishment; this is a particularly concrete instance of the section’s recompense held in wait.
The next punishment account says a cry seized the wrongdoers; it completes the three-day warning given in 11:65.
Ad’s punishment is described as a violent wind and humiliating chastisement in worldly life and the next, developing one of the section’s named exemplary peoples.
Thamud reject guidance and are seized by the humiliating lightning punishment; this supplies the same kind of exemplary return for the other named people.
The next ayah says the believers were saved; its own contribution is the boundary between those seized in the punishment and those delivered.

Ad see a cloud approaching their valleys and take it for rain, but it is the painful wind they had been promised. This specific reversal deepens the section’s use of Ad as an example of punishment rather than benefit.
The following ayah says the wind destroyed everything by its Lord’s command, leaving only the dwellings visible; it completes the cloud-to-punishment reversal.
Every person’s record is attached to them and opened on the Day of Resurrection; this makes the section’s preserved account an individual, unavoidable record.
The next ayah tells each person to read their record and says they suffice as their own reckoner, clarifying that no guardian can settle the final account for them.
A person has only what they strove for; this sharply individualizes the deeds whose return the section says is not diminished.
The following ayah says that striving will be seen, extending the personal account from action to disclosure.
Then each person is repaid fully; this is a precise parallel to the section’s promise that the due return remains intact.
The passage about underweighers continues by placing the record of the wicked in Sijjin, tying the short measure in 83:1–3 to a preserved adverse account.
This ayah identifies Sijjin as a written record, specifying how the wicked traders’ account is kept.
The other side of the surah says the record of the righteous is in Illiyyun, a direct counterpart to the wicked record and to the section’s assurance that good deeds are not lost.
The ayah calls Illiyyun a written record, specifying preservation for the righteous as the passage did for the wicked.
The next ayah says those brought near witness that record, completing the preserved account of good deeds.
The surah ends by asking whether the disbelievers have been recompensed for what they did; this is an explicit question of deferred return, though its immediate context is those who mocked believers.
Shuayb begins by ordering full measure and forbidding short measure; this is the positive counterpart to reducing another’s right, the secondary sense developed from the section’s وَتَرَهُ حَقَّهُ.
The next ayah commands weighing with a straight balance, completing the measure-and-right scene before 26:183 forbids reducing people’s due.
Shuayb likewise commands full measure and balance and forbids reducing people’s things; it is another concrete formulation of the section’s secondary “diminished right” sense.

Pharaoh’s people are exposed to the Fire morning and evening, then commanded into the harsher punishment when the Hour comes; the interval directly evokes the section’s punishment held ready at the mirsad.
The person given their record in the right hand faces an account; this develops the section’s preserved deeds into a personal reckoning.
The following ayah says that person receives an easy accounting, clarifying the outcome of the record in 84:7.
The next ayah says the person returns to their family rejoicing; this adds a family scene to the section’s final movement from judgment toward a welcomed return.
The person given the record from behind faces the other side of the account, a specific contrast to the return and approval at the end of the section.
The next ayah says this person calls for destruction, completing the adverse record’s immediate consequence.
The following ayah says they enter the Blaze, completing the adverse outcome paired with the record in 84:10.
